topic_tag: beam depth from a joint-variation load rule
subskill: joint variation, solve for a squared factor
prompt: For wooden beams cut from the same kind of lumber, the greatest load a rectangular beam can safely carry varies directly as the beam's width and as the square of the beam's depth, and varies inversely as the distance between the beam's supports. A beam 4 inches wide and 10 inches deep, resting on supports 12 feet apart, can safely carry 2,400 pounds. A beam that is 3 inches wide will rest on supports 14 feet apart and must safely carry 2,700 pounds. To the nearest tenth of an inch, what is the least depth this beam can have?
explanation: Write L = k·w·d²/s. From the first beam, k = 2,400(12)/(4·10²) = 72. For the new beam, 2,700 = 72(3)d²/14, so d² = 2,700(14)/216 = 175 and d ≈ 13.23, or 13.2 inches. The option "11.3" multiplies by the span instead of dividing by it (the load treated as varying directly with the distance between supports). The option "11.8" sets up the load ratio upside down, scaling by 2,400/2,700 instead of 2,700/2,400. The option "17.5" leaves the depth unsquared, scaling 10 inches directly by the combined factor.
quantity_asked: the least depth, in inches, of a 3-inch-wide beam on supports 14 feet apart that can safely carry 2,700 pounds.

distractor_kind.11.3: error path: treats the load as varying directly with the span (multiplies by 14/12 in the wrong place), d^2 = 128.6. (a) not a parameter extreme. (b) not an adjacent problem's answer at an edge: the width-ignored depth is 11.5 and the original 10 is the floor. (c) cheapest bound d > 10 (more load, less width, longer span all need more depth); 11.3 is strictly inside. (d) real inverted-variation error.
distractor_kind.11.8: error path: inverts the load ratio (2,400/2,700), d^2 = 138.3. (a) no extreme. (b) not an edge value. (c) strictly inside (10, 17.5). (d) real ratio-orientation error.
distractor_kind.17.5: error path: depth not squared, so the depth scales by the whole factor 1.75 instead of its square root. (a) no extreme. (b) not an edge of the interval. (c) strictly above key and inside any cheap estimate (one-step estimate d^2 = 100 x 1.125 x 4/3 x 7/6 is the solve itself). (d) real exponent-omission error.

bounds: d > 10 (larger load, narrower beam and longer span each require more depth)
mechanism: width times depth squared over span
least depth to carry a load
arith_class_check: No. All four are one-decimal values between 11 and 18; the key is the rounded square root of 175, not an integer or a round value.
one_sided_check: key interior (two distractors under, one over).
interior_parity_check: Interior by value: 11.8 and 13.2, both two-digit numbers with one non-zero decimal; neither is nicer.
trap_check: Clauses: "directly as the width" (ignoring it gives 11.5, under, not an option); "square of the depth" (ignoring the square gives 17.5, over); "inversely as the distance between supports" (read as direct gives 11.3, under). At most one option per clause; the clauses push both ways.

stated_rules.rule: load varies as the square of depth

self_audit.note: Interior key; errors on three different relations push both ways; d > 10 kills nothing; no option pair forced by the stem.

topic_tag: actual speed after larger tires are fitted to a car whose speedometer counts wheel turns
subskill: tire size code, diameter ratio, speedometer error
prompt: A tire size is written in the form W/A R D: W is the tire's width in millimeters, the height of the tire's sidewall is A percent of W, and D is the diameter of the wheel rim in inches. The overall diameter of the tire is the rim diameter plus twice the sidewall height (1 inch = 25.4 millimeters). A car's speedometer, which works by counting wheel revolutions, is accurate with the car's original 215/60 R16 tires. The owner replaces them with 225/70 R16 tires and does not adjust the speedometer. When the speedometer reads 60 miles per hour, what is the car's actual speed, to the nearest hundredth of a mile per hour?
explanation: The rim is 16(25.4) = 406.4 mm. Original sidewall: 0.60(215) = 129 mm, so the overall diameter is 406.4 + 2(129) = 664.4 mm. New sidewall: 0.70(225) = 157.5 mm, so the diameter is 406.4 + 2(157.5) = 721.4 mm. Each revolution now covers 721.4/664.4 times as far, so the actual speed is 60(721.4/664.4) ≈ 65.15 mph. The option "64.74" takes the 57-mm increase as a percent of the NEW diameter (7.90%) and adds that percent to 60. The option "63.19" adds only one sidewall height to the rim. The option "62.79" scales the speed by the ratio of the tire widths, 225/215.
quantity_asked: the car's actual speed, in miles per hour, when the speedometer reads 60.

distractor_kind.64.74: error path: diameter increase 57 mm taken as a percent of the new diameter (7.90%) and added to 60. (a) not a limiting case. (b) not an adjacent problem's edge. (c) one-step estimate: diameters about 26.2 in and 28.4 in, ratio about 1.085, speed about 65.1; 64.74 is 0.41 below the key and inside (60, 73.26). (d) real wrong-base error.
distractor_kind.63.19: error path: overall diameter = rim + ONE sidewall (406.4+129 and 406.4+157.5). (a) no extreme. (b) an adjacent setup, but strictly inside (60, 65.15). (c) inside. (d) real misreading of 'twice the sidewall'.
distractor_kind.62.79: error path: speed scaled by the width ratio 225/215. (a) no. (b) no. (c) inside (60, 73.26). (d) real wrong-quantity (wrong base) error: comparing widths instead of diameters.

bounds: v > 60 (larger tires cover more ground per revolution)
v < 60 x (157.5/129) = 73.26 (adding the same rim to both sidewall heights shrinks their ratio)
mechanism: tire size code to overall diameter
speedometer error after a tire change
speed proportional to wheel diameter at fixed revolutions
arith_class_check: No. All four are two-decimal speeds between 62 and 66 with non-zero hundredths; none integral or round.
one_sided_check: key largest; the three options come from a wrong base, a one-sidewall diameter and a width ratio. Natural errors also go OVER: leaving the rim in inches while the sidewalls are in mm (72.48) or scaling by the sidewall ratio (73.26). The stem does not fix the direction of the slips.
interior_parity_check: Interior by value: 63.19 and 64.74, both two-digit with two non-zero decimals; neither nicer.
cheap_bound_check: Cheapest bound: v > 60 (bigger tire), below all four. One step finer: v < 60 x sidewall ratio = 73.26, above all four. One-step estimate: diameters ~26.2 in and ~28.4 in give ~65.0-65.2, which the nearest distractor 64.74 (0.41 below) also sits near; nothing cheap separates 64.74 from 65.15. Distractors on the key's side of the 60 bound: all three.
trap_check: Clauses: sidewall is A% of W (ignored, sidewall = W: 61.43, under, not an option); rim in inches with 1 in = 25.4 mm (ignored: 72.48, over, not an option); diameter is rim + twice sidewall (one sidewall: 63.19, under, the only option from a clause). Not an additive chain.

63.19.step: overall diameter from rim and sidewall

62.79.step: choosing the quantity that scales the speed

counter_error.error_type: other: rim left in inches while sidewalls are in millimeters

stated_rules.rule: sidewall height is A percent of W
overall diameter = rim + twice the sidewall height

topic_tag: capacity error of a cylindrical tank from a mismeasured diameter
prompt: A cylindrical water tank has an actual inside diameter of 2.48 meters and an inside height of 3.10 meters. A technician measures the height correctly but records the inside diameter as 2.55 meters, and then uses these two measurements to compute the tank's capacity. To the nearest hundredth of a percent, by what percent of the tank's actual capacity is the computed capacity too large?
explanation: Capacity is πr²h, and only the diameter is wrong, so the computed capacity is (2.55/2.48)² ≈ 1.05725 times the actual capacity. It is too large by about 0.05725, or 5.72% of the actual capacity. The option "2.82" is the percent error in the diameter alone, 0.07/2.48, as if capacity changed in proportion to the diameter. The option "5.41" divides the excess by the computed capacity instead of the actual capacity. The option "8.71" scales the capacity by the cube of the diameter ratio, as if every dimension had grown.
quantity_asked: the excess of the computed capacity as a percent of the actual capacity.

distractor_kind.2.82: error path: linear scaling (the diameter's own percent error). (a) not a limiting case. (b) the diameter error is an intermediate quantity and sits below the key, but it is the natural first-instinct answer and is strictly inside (0, 8.71). (c) strictly below key. (d) real scaling error.
distractor_kind.5.41: error path: excess divided by the computed capacity. (a) no extreme. (b) not an edge value. (c) 0.31 below the key; the doubling estimate 2 x 2.82 = 5.65 separates them only for a student who knows (1+e)^2 > 1+2e, which is the squaring step itself. (d) real wrong-base error.
distractor_kind.8.71: error path: cubes the ratio as if the whole tank were scaled. (a) no extreme. (b) not an edge value. (c) above the doubling estimate. (d) real dimension-count error.

mechanism: cylinder capacity from a mismeasured diameter
arith_class_check: No. All four are two-decimal percents with non-zero final digits; none is an integer or round value.
interior_parity_check: Interior by value: 5.41 and 5.72, both one-digit with two non-zero decimals; neither is nicer.
trap_check: Clauses: "measures the height correctly" (ignoring it, i.e. scaling every dimension, gives 8.71, over); "of the tank's actual capacity" (using the computed capacity as base gives 5.41, under); squaring for area (dropping it gives 2.82, under). One option per clause; both directions.

2.82.error_type: other: linear instead of squared scaling

self_audit.note: Interior key; (1+e)^2 > 1+2e gives 5.65 between 5.41 and the key, but using it is the squaring step itself; 2.82 is the linear first instinct.

topic_tag: annual property tax bill with an assessment ratio, two exemptions and a flat fee
subskill: assessment ratio, ordered exemptions, tax rate
prompt: In a certain county, a home's assessed value is 85% of its market value. To find the taxable value, a homestead exemption of $24,500 is first subtracted from the assessed value, and then a senior exemption removes 10% of what remains. The annual tax bill is 1.31% of the taxable value plus a flat $78 county service fee. For a home with a market value of $384,600 owned by a senior who qualifies for both exemptions, what is the annual tax bill, to the nearest cent?
explanation: Assessed value: 0.85(384,600) = $326,910. Subtract the homestead exemption: 326,910 - 24,500 = $302,410. Remove 10%: 0.90(302,410) = $272,169. Tax: 0.0131(272,169) = $3,565.41, and the bill is 3,565.41 + 78 = $3,643.41. The option "3686.74" subtracts the $24,500 from the market value before taking 85%. The option "3611.32" applies the 10% senior exemption before subtracting the $24,500. The option "3535.75" combines the two percents into one, taking 85% - 10% = 75% of the market value before subtracting $24,500.
quantity_asked: the annual tax bill, in dollars, including the flat fee.

distractor_kind.3686.74: error path: the homestead exemption subtracted from the market value before the 85% assessment ratio. (a) not a limiting case. (b) not an edge. (c) one-step estimate: 1.31% of 0.9 x 0.85 x 384,600 is about 3,854, minus about 289 for the exemption, plus 78: about 3,643; 3686.74 inside (3,535, 3,932). (d) real wrong-base error.
distractor_kind.3611.32: error path: senior 10% taken from the full assessed value, then $24,500 subtracted (order reversed). (a) no. (b) not an edge. (c) inside. (d) real order error.
distractor_kind.3535.75: error path: the two percents combined additively (85% - 10% = 75% of market value). (a) no. (b) not an edge. (c) inside. (d) real additive-percent error.

mechanism: property tax from an assessment ratio
flat then percent exemption in a stated order
tax rate on taxable value plus a flat fee
arith_class_check: No. All four are dollar amounts with non-zero cents, none round.
interior_parity_check: Interior by value: 3611.32 and 3643.41, both four-digit dollars with non-zero cents; neither nicer.
trap_check: Clauses: 85% assessment ratio (exemption taken off market value instead: 3686.74, over); stated order homestead-then-senior (reversed: 3611.32, under); 10% of what remains (combined with the 85%: 3535.75, under); flat $78 fee (omitted: 3565.41, under, not an option). One distractor per clause.

3611.32.error_type: other: senior percent applied before the flat exemption

3535.75.step: combining the assessment ratio and the senior percent

topic_tag: third-year percent change needed to reach a target overall change
subskill: successive percent change, solve for the missing factor
prompt: The number of elk counted in a wildlife refuge increased by 13.5% from 2021 to 2022 and then decreased by 9.2% from 2022 to 2023. The refuge's managers want the 2024 count to be 9% greater than the 2021 count. To the nearest tenth of a percent, by what percent must the count increase from 2023 to 2024?
explanation: Let the 2021 count be N. The 2023 count is 1.135(0.908)N ≈ 1.0306N. The target is 1.09N, so the 2023-to-2024 factor is 1.09/1.0306 ≈ 1.0577, an increase of about 5.8%. The option "4.7" adds and subtracts the percents, 9 - 13.5 + 9.2. The option "4.9" divides by 1.092 for the decrease instead of multiplying by 0.908. The option "5.5" divides the needed increase, 0.0594N, by the 2024 target 1.09N instead of by the 2023 count.
quantity_asked: the percent increase from the 2023 count to the 2024 count that makes 2024 9% above 2021.

distractor_kind.4.7: error path: treats successive percents as additive. (a) not a limiting case. (b) it is the additive estimate, the floor a careful student might quote, but the key is not derivable from it without the products. (c) cheapest one-step estimate: 9 - 13.5 + 9.2 = 4.7 itself; key, 4.9 and 5.5 all lie on the key's side, so the estimate kills nothing beyond itself. (d) real additive-percent error.
distractor_kind.4.9: error path: divides by 1.092 for a 9.2% decrease. (a) no extreme. (b) not an edge value. (c) inside (4.7, 5.9). (d) real inverted-operation error.
distractor_kind.5.5: error path: needed increase taken as a percent of the 2024 target. (a) no extreme. (b) not an edge value. (c) inside. (d) real wrong-base error.

bounds: increase > 0 (the 2023 count, 1.0306N, is below the 1.09N target)
mechanism: missing third change to reach a target
arith_class_check: No. All four are one-decimal values between 4 and 6; the key is rounded from 5.766, and one distractor (4.7) is the exact one.
one_sided_check: key largest; three different error kinds (additive percents, division for a decrease, wrong base). The natural counter errors go over: giving the gap 1.09 - 1.0306 = 5.9 percentage points of the 2021 count (a wrong base the other way), and applying the 13.5% increase as division by 0.875 lowers the 2023 count and raises the answer. The stem does not signal a direction.
interior_parity_check: Interior by value: 4.9 and 5.5, both one-digit with one non-zero decimal; neither is nicer.
cheap_bound_check: Cheapest bound: the additive estimate 4.7 (a student who knows successive changes compound below the sum treats it as a floor). The key, 6.2 and 6.7 all lie on the key's side of it, so it kills only 4.7. Next: 1.09 - 1.0306 = 5.9 points is an upper bound only after computing 1.0306, which is the work; nothing cheap separates 5.5 from 5.8.
trap_check: Clauses: "increased by 13.5%" (ignored gives 20.0, over, not an option); "decreased by 9.2%" (applied by division gives 4.9, under; ignored gives -4.0, under, not an option); "9% greater than the 2021 count" (measured against the target gives 5.5, under; measured as points of the 2021 count gives 5.9, over, not an option). Only 4.7 comes from a whole-method error.

self_audit.note: Largest key; the counter error is the same wrong-base slip in the other direction (points of 2021), 0.2 above; additive floor kills only itself.

topic_tag: screen area of two televisions from diagonal size and aspect ratio
subskill: rectangle from diagonal and side ratio, percent less
prompt: A television's screen size is the length of the diagonal of its rectangular screen, and its aspect ratio is the ratio of the screen's width to its height. Television A has a 65-inch screen with an aspect ratio of 16:9. Television B has a 58-inch screen with an aspect ratio of 4:3. By what percent is the area of Television B's screen less than the area of Television A's screen, to the nearest hundredth of a percent?
explanation: For a screen with diagonal d and sides in the ratio a:b, the sides are da/√(a²+b²) and db/√(a²+b²), so the area is d²ab/(a²+b²). A: 65²(144)/337 ≈ 1805.31 square inches. B: 58²(12)/25 = 1614.72 square inches. B is less by (1805.31 - 1614.72)/1805.31 ≈ 0.1056, or 10.56%. The option "11.81" divides the difference by B's area instead of A's. The option "10.77" uses the ratio of the diagonals, 58/65, as the ratio of the areas. The option "15.37" takes each side as a share of the diagonal itself (width 16/25 of 65, height 9/25 of 65; width 4/7 of 58, height 3/7 of 58), as if the sides added up to the diagonal.
quantity_asked: the percent by which Television B's screen area is less than Television A's screen area.

distractor_kind.11.81: error path: the area difference taken as a percent of B's area (percent more, not percent less). (a) not a limiting case. (b) not an adjacent problem's edge. (c) cheapest one-step bound: B is taller than A (34.8 in vs 31.9 in), so B's area deficit is below its width deficit, 18.10; 11.81 inside (0, 18.10). (d) real wrong-base error.
distractor_kind.10.77: error path: area ratio taken as the diagonal ratio 58/65 (no squaring, no aspect). (a) no extreme. (b) not on a bound: the diagonal ratio is neither an upper nor a lower bound here. (c) inside, 0.21 above the key. (d) real linear-for-area error.
distractor_kind.15.37: error path: sides found as fractions a/(a+b) and b/(a+b) of the diagonal, as if the sides summed to it. (a) no. (b) not an edge. (c) inside (0, 18.10). (d) real misconception about splitting the diagonal in the aspect ratio.

15.37.error_kind: diagonal split in the aspect ratio

bounds: 0 < v < 18.10 (B's width is 18.10% less than A's, and B is taller)
mechanism: rectangle sides from a diagonal and a side ratio
television screen area from screen size and aspect ratio
arith_class_check: No. All four are two-decimal percents with non-zero hundredths; none integral or round.
one_sided_check: key smallest; distractors from a wrong base, a linear-for-area slip and a diagonal-split misconception (three kinds). A natural error goes UNDER: adding the separate width change (-18.10%) and height change (+9.20%) gives 8.89. The stem does not fix the direction of the slips.
interior_parity_check: Interior by value: 10.77 and 11.81, both two-digit with two non-zero decimals; neither nicer.
cheap_bound_check: Cheapest bound: B's width is 18.10% less than A's but B is taller, so v < 18.10 - above all four, kills nothing. The diagonal ratio 58/65 (10.77) is not a bound: B's squarer shape gives it more area per diagonal, but squaring the diagonal ratio moves the other way, and which wins needs the computation. Nearest distractor 10.77 is 0.21 above the key; nothing cheap separates them. All three distractors lie on the key's side of the 18.10 bound.

10.77.error_type: other: diagonal ratio used as the area ratio

topic_tag: gas pressure under inverse variation after two volume changes
prompt: At a constant temperature, the pressure of a gas trapped in a cylinder varies inversely as the volume of the gas. A piston first decreases the volume of the gas by 18%. The piston is then pulled back so that the volume increases by 7% of that decreased volume. To the nearest hundredth of a percent, by what percent is the final pressure greater than the original pressure?
explanation: The final volume is 0.82(1.07) = 0.8774 times the original volume. Because pressure varies inversely as volume, the final pressure is 1/0.8774 ≈ 1.1397 times the original pressure, about 13.97% greater. The option "9.74" turns each volume change into the opposite pressure change (up 18%, then down 7%). The option "12.36" takes the 7% increase from the original volume, so the final volume is 0.89 of it. The option "13.41" handles the 18% decrease correctly but turns the 7% volume increase into a 7% pressure decrease.
quantity_asked: the percent by which the final pressure exceeds the original pressure.

distractor_kind.9.74: error path: inverse variation read as 'opposite percent change' at both steps. (a) not a limiting case. (b) not an adjacent setup's edge value. (c) cheapest one-step estimate 0.82 x 1.07 ~ 0.88, 1/0.88 ~ 1.136: the interval it supports is roughly (13, 14.5); 9.74 is outside it but the estimate is the work. (d) real misreading of inverse variation.
distractor_kind.12.36: error path: second change taken as 7% of the original volume. (a) no extreme. (b) not an edge. (c) below the estimate. (d) real wrong-base error.
distractor_kind.13.41: error path: first step correct, second step turned into a 7% pressure decrease. (a) no extreme. (b) not an edge. (c) 0.56 below the key; the one-step estimate 13.6 sits between them and is nearer 13.41. (d) real partial misreading of inverse variation.

13.41.error_kind: opposite percent at the second step

mechanism: piston compresses then expands a gas
arith_class_check: No. All four are two-decimal percents between 9 and 14 with non-zero hundredths; none is an integer or a round value.
one_sided_check: key largest; distractors from two different misreadings and one wrong base. Natural counter errors go over: ignoring the second (expanding) step gives 21.95, and turning the 7% increase into division by 0.93 on pressure gives 31.13; the stem gives no direction.
interior_parity_check: Interior by value: 12.36 and 13.41, both two-digit with two non-zero decimals; neither is nicer.

One option per clause reading.

9.74.step: converting volume changes to pressure changes
9.74.error_type: other: opposite percent for inverse variation

topic_tag: monthly sales from a pay raise under base salary plus threshold commission
subskill: commission above a threshold, percent increase in pay
prompt: Each month, a salesperson is paid a base salary of $1,850 plus a commission of 4% of the amount by which that month's sales exceed $24,000. In April, the salesperson's sales were $48,700. The salesperson's total pay in May was 12% greater than the total pay in April. What were the salesperson's sales in May, to the nearest dollar?
explanation: April pay is 1,850 + 0.04(48,700 - 24,000) = 1,850 + 988 = $2,838. May pay is 1.12(2,838) = $3,178.56, so the May commission is 3,178.56 - 1,850 = $1,328.56. That is 4% of 1,328.56/0.04 = $33,214 above $24,000, so May sales were $57,214. The option "58375" finds May pay as 2,838/0.88, treating April pay as 12% less than May pay. The option "60094" ignores the $24,000 threshold and applies the 4% to all sales in both months. The option "65487" scales April sales by the ratio of the commissions, 1,328.56/988, as if sales were proportional to commission.
quantity_asked: total sales in May, in dollars.

topic_tag: price per square inch of topped area for two round pizzas with a bare crust
subskill: unit price per area, annulus, percent less
prompt: A pizzeria sells a large round pizza 16 inches in diameter for $19.49 and a small round pizza 12 inches in diameter for $12.79. On each pizza, a crust 1 inch wide around the edge has no topping, and the rest of the pizza is evenly covered with topping. Measured by price per square inch of topped area, by what percent is the large pizza cheaper than the small pizza, to the nearest hundredth of a percent?
explanation: The topped regions are circles of radius 8 - 1 = 7 in and 6 - 1 = 5 in, with areas 49π and 25π square inches. Large: 19.49/(49π) ≈ $0.12661 per square inch; small: 12.79/(25π) ≈ $0.16285 per square inch. The large is cheaper by 1 - 0.12661/0.16285 ≈ 0.2225, or 22.25%. The option "28.62" divides the same price difference by the LARGE pizza's price per square inch. The option "23.81" finds each crust's area as its outer circumference times 1 inch (16π and 12π), giving topped areas 48π and 24π. The option "32.27" removes 2 inches from each radius (the 2-inch reduction in diameter applied to the radius).

topic_tag: stain for three coats with coverage that improves coat by coat
prompt: A rectangular deck measures 20 feet by 22 feet, and its top surface will receive three coats of stain. For the first coat, on bare wood, 1 gallon of stain covers 250 square feet. For the second coat, 1 gallon covers 40% more area than it did on the first coat. For the third coat, 1 gallon covers 20% more area than it did on the second coat. To the nearest hundredth of a gallon, how many gallons of stain are needed for all three coats?
explanation: The deck's area is 20(22) = 440 square feet. A gallon covers 250 square feet on the first coat, 1.40(250) = 350 on the second, and 1.20(350) = 420 on the third. The stain needed is 440/250 + 440/350 + 440/420 ≈ 1.760 + 1.257 + 1.048 ≈ 4.06 gallons. The option "3.88" averages the three coverage rates (340 square feet per gallon) and uses that rate for all three coats. The option "3.66" treats each increase in coverage as the same percent decrease in stain (0.60 and then 0.80 times the previous coat's stain). The option "4.02" finds the first two coats correctly but uses 0.80 times the second coat's stain for the third coat instead of dividing by 1.20.
quantity_asked: the total gallons of stain for three coats on the 440-square-foot deck.

distractor_kind.3.88: error path: averages the three coverage rates (250, 350, 420) and applies 340 sq ft/gal to every coat. (a) not a limiting case. (b) not an edge: the interval for three coats is (3 x 440/420, 3 x 440/250) = (3.14, 5.28); 3.88 is strictly inside. (c) the rate average is the cheapest one-rate estimate and lands here, below the key. (d) real averaging-of-rates error.
distractor_kind.3.66: error path: 40% more coverage taken as 40% less stain, then 20% more as 20% less. (a) no extreme. (b) inside (3.14, 5.28). (c) inside. (d) real inverted-percent error at both steps.
distractor_kind.4.02: error path: first two coats correct, third coat taken as 0.80 of the second coat's stain. (a) no extreme. (b) inside. (c) 0.04 below the key. (d) real inverted-percent error at the last step.
